title: Index plane — we consume Db2's DiskANN, we don't get to choose it: prove the index engages, and measure when it doesn't
description:
Second of seven plane epics (see `project-management/design/ADVANCED_MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` and `project-management/AI_NATIVE_AGILE.md`).

**Invariant this plane owns:** indexes are consistent with the store at read-your-writes.

**This epic opens by retracting a recommendation.** `project-management/design/ADVANCED_MEMORY_ARCHITECTURE.md` Phase 5.1/5.2 proposed a `VectorIndex` protocol with pluggable `hnswlib` / `diskann` backends. That was written without knowing what Db2's vector index actually is. It is DiskANN. Db2 12.1.5 (GA 25 June 2026) ships DiskANN-powered vector indexing; the catalog exposes it as `SYSCAT.INDEXES.INDEXTYPE = 'VANN'` and EXPLAIN labels the access as `VECIDX`. The consequence is not a disappointment but a scope correction: **we already have the billion-scale index the research doc was reaching for, and we cannot tune, replace, or contribute to its internals.** There is no `efSearch`, no `M`, no rebuild policy we control. A pluggable-backend abstraction would therefore add a seam with nothing to put behind it.

All the remaining leverage in this plane is on our side of the boundary: making sure Db2's DiskANN is actually *engaged*, shaping the data and the predicates so it stays engaged, and measuring recall when it doesn't. Reading the current `repositories/base.py::search()` against what Db2 requires turns up five concrete suspicions, none yet confirmed against a live database — which is why the first two stories are spikes and everything else is ranked behind them.

**A. The zero-vector filter is non-sargable and applied to the indexed column.** ORC-2 added
`AND VECTOR_SERIALIZE(embedding) != VECTOR_SERIALIZE(CAST('<zeros>' AS VECTOR(d,FLOAT32)))`
to the ID-ranking query, for a correct reason: chunked parent rows store a zero-vector sentinel to satisfy `NOT NULL`, and COSINE distance against a zero vector raises SQL0801N. But a function call wrapped around the indexed column in the WHERE clause is the textbook shape that stops an index being used, or degrades it to a full FETCH of every candidate. If this predicate defeats `VECIDX`, then `FETCH APPROX` has been silently costing us the index on every single search — including in the benchmark numbers already published. Unconfirmed, high impact, cheap to test: VIDX-1.

**B. Sentinel rows pollute the graph even when the filter works.** Every chunked parent is a node sitting at the origin of the DiskANN proximity graph — equidistant from nothing useful, occupying index space and distorting neighbourhoods. The right fix is to stop putting them in the indexed column at all; the wrong fix is more residual predicates.

**C. The APPROX to EXACT fallback is silent, and that is a benchmark-integrity problem.** When Db2 raises SQL0104N on the `APPROX` keyword, `search()` logs a warning and retries without it. That is the correct runtime behaviour and should stay. What is not correct is that the caller — and therefore the benchmark report — has no way to know a run labelled APPROX actually measured EXACT. This is the same class of defect EPIC-11 was raised for, and the fix is to surface the effective mode in result metadata rather than only in a log line.

**D. Db2 hands us a recall harness for free, and we aren't using it.** The same query under `FETCH EXACT` and `FETCH APPROX` yields ground truth and approximation over identical data, so recall@k is a set intersection — no labelled dataset, no judge, no embedding calls beyond the query. For a plane whose entire quality story is 'how much recall are we trading for latency', this is the measurement instrument, and it belongs in `benchmarks/` before any tuning story is allowed to claim a win.

**E. The optimizer may not be choosing the index in our tests at all.** Published testing of Db2 vector indexes needed explicit `OPTGUIDELINES` to force `IXSCAN` on small tables, because on small cardinalities a table scan genuinely costs less. Most of this repo's live-Db2 tests run against small tables. A green test suite is therefore *not* evidence that the index path works — it may be evidence that the index path has never once executed. Also confirmed from the same source and worth stating because it is a silent-failure mode: vector indexes are only used when the vector column is `NOT NULL`, which our DDL does satisfy.

**F. Filtered searches get no candidate inflation.** `fetch_k = min(top_k * 4, 800)` is applied only when `hybrid=True`. A scope-filtered, metadata-filtered, confidence-filtered APPROX search asks for exactly `top_k` candidates and then filters them — the classic post-filter under-fetch, where a selective predicate silently returns fewer than `top_k` results, or none. Scope columns (`tenant_id`/`agent_id`/`user_id`/`thread_id`) are extremely high-selectivity by construction, so this is the common case, not the edge case.

**Two tradeoffs gated behind spikes:** what `CREATE VECTOR INDEX ... WITH DISTANCE` actually exposes as build-time knobs is documented loosely as 'clauses to determine physical properties and the way the index is built' and needs enumerating against the real product (VIDX-2); and per-scope index partitioning is theoretically the right answer to filtered ANN — it converts the hardest filtered case into the easy unfiltered one and closes the shared-index isolation gap — but may be unavailable, or may create a thousand-tiny-indexes pathology (VIDX-7).

**Scope boundary:** the vector index only. Sparse/BM25 indexing is EPIC-29 (RTRV-2/RTRV-3) because it is a retrieval-quality question, not a vector-index question. Nothing in this epic changes result semantics; VIDX-4 changes what is *reported* about results, not the results.

**Depends on:** nothing hard. **Blocks:** any EPIC-29 story claiming a latency win, since without VIDX-3 there is no recall baseline to hold constant.
